la.subspace.title: Subspace tests
la.subspace.subject: Linear Algebra
la.subspace.check: Check 0 is in the set, then closure under + and scalar multiples; span and null spaces always pass, affine sets (=b≠0) never do.

la.independence.title: Linear independence
la.independence.subject: Linear Algebra
la.independence.check: Put the vectors as columns; independent iff rank = number of vectors (square case: det ≠ 0).

la.basis-dim.title: Basis and dimension
la.basis-dim.subject: Linear Algebra
la.basis-dim.check: dim = number of pivots after row reduction; for a solution set, dim = n − (number of independent constraints).

la.special-matrices.title: Special matrices: symmetric, skew, idempotent, nilpotent
la.special-matrices.subject: Linear Algebra
la.special-matrices.check: Use the defining identity (Aᵀ=±A, A²=A, Aᵏ=0) to pin eigenvalues, det and trace; test claims with a 2×2 counterexample.

la.block-matrix.title: Block and partitioned products
la.block-matrix.subject: Linear Algebra
la.block-matrix.check: Multiply blocks like scalars but keep the order; check every block size matches.

la.transpose-inverse.title: Transpose and inverse rules
la.transpose-inverse.subject: Linear Algebra
la.transpose-inverse.check: (AB)ᵀ=BᵀAᵀ, (AB)⁻¹=B⁻¹A⁻¹, (cA)⁻¹=A⁻¹/c; never distribute an inverse over a sum.

la.rank-rref.title: Rank by row reduction
la.rank-rref.subject: Linear Algebra
la.rank-rref.check: Row reduce fully, then count pivots. A row that is a combination of others (not just a multiple) also vanishes.

la.rank-nullity.title: Rank–nullity
la.rank-nullity.subject: Linear Algebra
la.rank-nullity.check: For m×n A: rank + nullity = n (columns). Nullity of Aᵀ = m − rank.

la.solvability.title: Existence and uniqueness of Ax = b; Gaussian elimination
la.solvability.subject: Linear Algebra
la.solvability.check: Consistent iff rank A = rank [A|b]; unique iff also rank = n. Shape: rank = m ⇒ always solvable, rank = n ⇒ at most one solution.

la.det-props.title: Determinant properties
la.det-props.subject: Linear Algebra
la.det-props.check: det(cA)=cⁿdet A, det(A⁻¹)=1/det A, det(Aᵀ)=det A; row swap flips sign, row addition changes nothing.

la.det-poly.title: Determinant of p(A) via eigenvalues
la.det-poly.subject: Linear Algebra
la.det-poly.check: det p(A) = product of p(λᵢ) over all eigenvalues; never plug det A into p.

la.eig-trace-det.title: Eigenvalues from trace and determinant
la.eig-trace-det.subject: Linear Algebra
la.eig-trace-det.check: Sum of eigenvalues = trace, product = det. Diagonal entries are eigenvalues only for triangular matrices.

la.eig-transform.title: Eigenvalues of Aᵏ, A⁻¹, A + cI, cA
la.eig-transform.subject: Linear Algebra
la.eig-transform.check: Same eigenvector; λ becomes λᵏ, 1/λ, λ + c, cλ. Transform every eigenvalue, then answer.

la.rank-one.title: Rank-one matrices uvᵀ
la.rank-one.subject: Linear Algebra
la.rank-one.check: uvᵀ has eigenvalues vᵀu and 0 (n−1 times); I + xxᵀ has 1 + xᵀx and 1s.

la.rank-gm.title: Algebraic vs geometric multiplicity
la.rank-gm.subject: Linear Algebra
la.rank-gm.check: Row reduce A − λI, count pivots; GM = n − rank. Diagonalizable iff GM = AM for every eigenvalue.

la.eigvec-check.title: Checking eigenvectors
la.eigvec-check.subject: Linear Algebra
la.eigvec-check.check: Compute Av and see if it is a multiple of v; scaled eigenvectors still count. Equal row sums s ⇒ A·1 = s·1.

la.projection.title: Projection matrices
la.projection.subject: Linear Algebra
la.projection.check: P² = P ⇒ eigenvalues 0/1 and rank = trace; orthogonal projection also has Pᵀ = P. Onto a line: P = aaᵀ/(aᵀa).

la.orthogonal.title: Orthogonal matrices
la.orthogonal.subject: Linear Algebra
la.orthogonal.check: QᵀQ = I: preserves length, det = ±1, every (complex) eigenvalue has |λ| = 1.

la.definiteness.title: Quadratic forms, definiteness and Gram matrices
la.definiteness.subject: Linear Algebra
la.definiteness.check: Halve the cross terms to build the symmetric matrix, then check eigenvalue signs (or leading minors). AᵀA is PD iff columns independent.

la.rayleigh.title: Rayleigh quotient extremes
la.rayleigh.subject: Linear Algebra
la.rayleigh.check: For symmetric A, max/min of xᵀAx on ‖x‖ = 1 are λmax/λmin, attained at eigenvectors.

la.lu.title: LU decomposition
la.lu.subject: Linear Algebra
la.lu.check: Eliminate column by column; multipliers lᵢⱼ = (entry)/(pivot) fill L, the reduced rows form U. det A = product of U's diagonal.

la.svd.title: Singular values and SVD
la.svd.subject: Linear Algebra
la.svd.check: σᵢ = √(eigenvalues of AᵀA); rank = number of non-zero σ; uvᵀ has σ = ‖u‖‖v‖; symmetric PSD ⇒ σ = λ.

questions.stem: Which of the following subsets of $\mathbb{R}^3$ are subspaces?

options.why: Union of two planes. $(1,0,0)+(0,1,0)=(1,1,0)$ has $xy=1$, so it is not closed under addition.
It is the null space of the $1\times 3$ matrix $(1\;2\;-1)$; null spaces always contain $0$ and are closed under $+$ and scaling.
A span is always a subspace: it contains $0$ and every combination of combinations is a combination.
Affine plane: $(0,0,0)$ gives $0\neq 1$, so the zero vector is missing.

questions.solution:
1. Test $0$ first: the plane $x+y+z=1$ fails.
2. Nonlinear conditions ($xy=0$) usually fail closure; find two members whose sum leaves the set.
3. Null spaces and spans pass automatically.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be a real $3\times 4$ matrix and $b\neq 0$. Which of the following are subspaces (of the stated space)?

options.text: The set of all $2\times 2$ real symmetric matrices, in $\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}$
options.why: $0$ is symmetric, and $(A+B)^T=A+B$, $(cA)^T=cA$ for symmetric $A,B$.
$A0=0\neq b$, so $0$ is not a solution. Solution sets of $Ax=b$ with $b\neq0$ are shifted (affine) sets.
Closed under addition but not under scaling: $(-1)\cdot(1,0,0,0)$ has $x_1=-1$.

options.text: The set of all invertible $2\times 2$ matrices, in $\mathbb{R}^{2\times 2}$
options.why: The zero matrix is not invertible; also $I+(-I)=0$ leaves the set.

questions.solution: Only the symmetric matrices pass all three checks: contains $0$, closed under $+$, closed under scalar multiples (including negative scalars).

questions.stem: Let $A$ be a real $3\times 4$ matrix and $b\in\mathbb{R}^3$ a non-zero vector. Which set is always a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^4$?

options.why: The null space: if $Ax=0$ and $Ay=0$ then $A(x+cy)=0$.
Contains $0$ but is not closed under scaling: $e_1$ is in the set, $2e_1$ is not.
Adding $0$ by hand does not give closure: if $Ax=b$ then $A(2x)=2b\neq b$.
Contains no zero vector since $A0=0\ne b$; it is a translate of the null space.

questions.solution: Only the null space satisfies all three tests. Patching in $0$ does not repair an affine set.

questions.stem: For a real constant $k$ let $W_k=\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{R}^3: x+y=k,\; z=2x\}$. Which statements are true?

options.why: Two independent equations in 3 unknowns leave $3-2=1$ free variable: $W_0=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,2)\}$.

options.text: $W_k$ is a subspace for every $k$, because it is defined by linear equations
options.why: Linear equations with a non-zero right side give an affine set: $(0,0,0)$ fails $x+y=k$ when $k\neq 0$.

options.text: $W_3$ is a line in $\mathbb{R}^3$ that does not pass through the origin
options.why: $W_3=(3,0,6)+t(1,-1,2)$: a line parallel to $W_0$, shifted off the origin.
For $k=0$ both conditions are homogeneous linear equations, so $W_0$ is a null space.

questions.solution:
1. $W_k$ contains $0$ only when $k=0$.
2. $W_0$: $y=-x$, $z=2x$, so $W_0=\operatorname{span}\{(1,-1,2)\}$, dimension 1.
3. $W_3$ is $W_0$ shifted by the particular point $(3,0,6)$.

questions.stem: Let $P_2$ be the space of real polynomials of degree at most 2. Which subsets are subspaces of $P_2$?

options.why: The zero polynomial is missing, and $x^2+(-x^2+x)=x$ has degree 1.
This is the set of constant polynomials, the null space of the linear map $p\mapsto p'$.
$(p+cq)(1)=p(1)+cq(1)=0$, and the zero polynomial satisfies it.
The zero polynomial has $p(0)=0\ne1$; the sum of two members has value $2$ at $0$.

questions.solution: Conditions of the form $L(p)=0$ with $L$ linear (evaluation, derivative) give subspaces. $L(p)=1$ or a degree condition does not.

questions.stem: For what value of $k$ are the vectors $(1,1,0)^T$, $(0,1,1)^T$ and $(1,0,k)^T$ linearly dependent?

traps.why: Sign slip in the cofactor expansion: the determinant is $k+1$, not $k-1$.
Assumed a zero entry makes the set dependent; with $k=0$ the determinant is $1\neq0$.

questions.solution:
1. Put the vectors as columns: $\det\begin{pmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&k\end{pmatrix}=1\cdot(k-0)-0+1\cdot(1-0)=k+1$.
2. Dependent iff $k+1=0$, so $k=-1$.
3. Check: $(1,0,-1)=(1,1,0)-(0,1,1)$.

questions.stem: Which statements about vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ are true?

options.text: Any set of 4 vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ is linearly dependent
options.why: At most 3 pivots exist in a $3\times4$ matrix, so at least one column is free.

options.text: If $v_1,v_2$ are independent and $v_3\notin\operatorname{span}\{v_1,v_2\}$, then $\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}$ is independent
options.why: A dependency with $c_3\neq0$ would put $v_3$ in the span; with $c_3=0$ it would be a dependency of $v_1,v_2$. (Merely pairwise non-parallel would not be enough: $(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(1,1,0)$.)

options.text: Every non-empty subset of a linearly independent set is linearly independent
options.why: A dependency among the subset would also be a dependency of the full set (pad with zero coefficients).

options.text: Any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent
options.why: $1\cdot 0=0$ is a non-trivial combination giving zero.

questions.solution: All four hold. Independence is about the whole set: adding a vector outside the current span keeps it independent; pairwise checks alone are not enough.

questions.stem: Vectors $v_1, v_2, v_3$ are linearly independent. Which of the following sets is linearly **dependent**?

options.why: The three vectors add to $0$: a non-trivial dependency. The coefficient matrix has determinant $0$.
Coefficient matrix has determinant $2\neq0$, so this set is independent (true over the reals).
Coefficient matrix determinant $2\cdot3\cdot1=6\neq0$; scaling does not create a dependency.
Triangular coefficient matrix with determinant $1$; you can recover each $v_i$ by subtraction.

questions.solution:
1. Write each new vector in terms of $v_1,v_2,v_3$; the new set is independent iff the coefficient matrix is invertible.
2. Determinants: sums $2$, differences $0$, cumulative sums $1$, scaled set $6$.
3. Only the cyclic differences fail: $(v_1-v_2)+(v_2-v_3)+(v_3-v_1)=0$.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be a real $5\times 3$ matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(A)=3$. Which statements are true?

options.text: The columns of $A$ are linearly independent
options.why: 3 columns and rank 3: every column holds a pivot.
$\operatorname{rank}(A^TA)=\operatorname{rank}(A)=3$, and $A^TA$ is $3\times3$.

options.text: The rows of $A$ are linearly independent
options.why: 5 rows in a row space of dimension 3: at least 2 rows depend on the others.
Independent columns mean the only combination giving $0$ is the trivial one (nullity $=3-3=0$).

questions.solution: Rank 3 equals the number of columns, so the columns are independent and the null space is $\{0\}$. Rank 3 is less than the number of rows, so the rows are dependent.

questions.stem: Find the dimension of the subspace of $\mathbb{R}^4$ spanned by $$(1,2,0,1),\;(2,4,1,3),\;(0,0,1,1),\;(3,6,1,4).$$

traps.why: Counted the vectors (or non-zero rows) without row reducing.

questions.solution:
1. Stack as rows and reduce: $R_2-2R_1=(0,0,1,1)=R_3$; $R_4-3R_1=(0,0,1,1)$.
2. After elimination only two non-zero rows remain.
3. Dimension $=2$, basis $\{(1,2,0,1),(0,0,1,1)\}$.

questions.stem: Find the dimension of $W=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^5: x_1+x_2+x_3=0,\; x_4=x_5\}$.

traps.why: Reported the number of constraints instead of $n$ minus the number of constraints.
Counted only one of the two independent constraints.

questions.solution:
1. $W$ is the null space of a $2\times5$ matrix with 2 independent rows.
2. $\dim W = 5-2 = 3$ (free: $x_2, x_3, x_5$).

questions.stem: Which of the following dimension statements about spaces of real $3\times 3$ matrices are true?

options.text: Upper-triangular matrices form a space of dimension 6
options.why: Entries on or above the diagonal: $3+2+1=6$.

options.text: Symmetric matrices form a space of dimension 6
options.why: Free entries: 3 diagonal + 3 above the diagonal.

options.text: Matrices with trace $0$ form a space of dimension 6
options.why: Trace $0$ is one linear constraint on 9 entries, so the dimension is $9-1=8$.

options.text: Skew-symmetric matrices form a space of dimension 6
options.why: Counted the diagonal as free, as for symmetric matrices; $a_{ii}=-a_{ii}$ forces it to $0$, leaving 3 free entries.

questions.solution: Count free entries. Symmetric $n(n+1)/2=6$, skew $n(n-1)/2=3$, upper triangular $6$, trace-zero $n^2-1=8$.

questions.stem: Let $V$ be a vector space of dimension $n$. Which statements are true?

options.text: Some spanning set of $V$ has fewer than $n$ vectors
options.why: Every spanning set has at least $\dim V$ vectors; fewer vectors span a space of dimension less than $n$.

options.text: Any $n$ vectors that span $V$ form a basis
options.why: A spanning set of size $\dim V$ cannot contain a redundant vector, so it is independent.

options.text: Any $n$ linearly independent vectors in $V$ form a basis
options.why: An independent set of size $\dim V$ automatically spans.
A basis of the subspace is 4 independent vectors in $\mathbb{R}^4$, hence a basis of $\mathbb{R}^4$.

questions.solution: With the right count ($n$), either independence or spanning is enough for a basis. Spanning sets have at least $n$ vectors; independent sets have at most $n$.

questions.stem: $W_1$ and $W_2$ are subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^5$ with $\dim W_1=3$ and $\dim W_2=4$. The smallest possible value of $\dim(W_1\cap W_2)$ is

options.why: $\dim(W_1\cap W_2)=3+4-\dim(W_1+W_2)\ge 7-5=2$, and 2 is attained (e.g. coordinate subspaces).
Arithmetic slip in $3+4-5$, or used $\dim(W_1+W_2)=6$, which exceeds 5.
Ignored that both live in $\mathbb{R}^5$: $\dim(W_1+W_2)\le5$ forces overlap.
That is the largest possible value (when $W_1\subseteq W_2$), not the smallest.

questions.solution:
1. $\dim(W_1\cap W_2)=\dim W_1+\dim W_2-\dim(W_1+W_2)$.
2. $W_1+W_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^5$, so the intersection has dimension at least $7-5=2$.
3. Example: $W_1=\operatorname{span}\{e_1,e_2,e_3\}$, $W_2=\operatorname{span}\{e_2,e_3,e_4,e_5\}$.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ real matrix with $A^2=A$, $A\neq 0$ and $A\neq I$. Which statements are true?

options.why: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ satisfies $A^2=A$ but is not symmetric (an oblique projection).
If $A$ were invertible, multiplying $A^2=A$ by $A^{-1}$ gives $A=I$, which is excluded.
$(2A)^2=4A^2=4A\neq2A$; scaling breaks idempotence. (It is $I-A$ that is again idempotent.)
$Av=\lambda v\Rightarrow A^2v=\lambda^2v=\lambda v$, so $\lambda^2=\lambda$.

questions.solution: Idempotent means projection: eigenvalues 0/1, $\operatorname{rank}=\operatorname{trace}$, singular unless $A=I$. Symmetry is an extra property (orthogonal projection).

questions.stem: Let $N$ be a non-zero $n\times n$ real matrix with $N^k=0$ for some $k\ge2$. Which statements are true?

options.why: Eigenvalues of $I+N$ are all $1$, so $\det(I+N)=1$. Explicitly $(I+N)^{-1}=I-N+N^2-\dots$
A symmetric matrix is diagonalizable; with all eigenvalues $0$ it would equal $0$, but $N\neq0$.
$Nv=\lambda v\Rightarrow 0=N^kv=\lambda^kv$, so $\lambda=0$.
Zero eigenvalues do not make a matrix zero: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has rank 1.

questions.solution:
1. Nilpotent $\Rightarrow$ all eigenvalues $0$, so trace $0$ and det $0$.
2. Rank is not determined by eigenvalues alone.
3. Symmetric + nilpotent forces $N=0$.

questions.stem: $A$ is a real $3\times 3$ skew-symmetric matrix ($A^T=-A$). Then $\det(A)$ is

options.text: the sum of squares of the entries above the diagonal
options.why: Generalised from the $2\times2$ case $\det\begin{pmatrix}0&a\\-a&0\end{pmatrix}=a^2$; for odd $n$ the sign argument forces $0$.
$\det A=\det A^T=\det(-A)=(-1)^3\det A$, so $\det A=0$. Works for every odd $n$.

options.text: any real number, depending on the entries
options.why: Used $\det(-A)=-\det A$ without the power: the correct rule is $\det(-A)=(-1)^n\det A$.
Confused skew-symmetric with orthogonal ($\det=\pm1$).

questions.solution:
1. $\det(A^T)=\det A$.
2. $\det(-A)=(-1)^n\det A=-\det A$ for $n=3$.
3. So $\det A=-\det A$, i.e. $\det A=0$.

questions.stem: Let $A$ and $B$ be real $n\times n$ matrices. Which statements are always true?

options.text: If $A$ and $B$ are symmetric, $AB$ is symmetric
options.why: $(AB)^T=BA$, which equals $AB$ only if they commute. Example: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ give $AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.solution: Transpose each expression and use $(XY)^T=Y^TX^T$. Products of symmetric matrices are symmetric only when they commute.

questions.stem: For which value of $k$ is $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&k\\-2&-2\end{pmatrix}$ idempotent ($A^2=A$)?

traps.why: Sign slip in $\det A=3(-2)-k(-2)=-6+2k$; wrote $-6-2k=0$.
Used rank $=$ trace $=1$ and stopped; trace is $1$ for every $k$, so it does not fix $k$.

questions.solution:
1. A non-trivial idempotent $2\times2$ matrix has eigenvalues $0,1$: trace $1$ (true for all $k$) and $\det=0$.
2. $\det A=-6+2k=0\Rightarrow k=3$.
3. Check: $A^2=\begin{pmatrix}9-2k&k\\-2&4-2k\end{pmatrix}=A$ at $k=3$.

questions.stem: Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}I_2&B\\0&I_2\end{pmatrix}$ with $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(1,4)$ entry of $M^5$.

traps.why: Read the $(1,4)$ entry of $M$ itself; forgot that the off-diagonal block grows with the power.
Raised the entry to the 5th power ($2^5$) instead of multiplying the block by 5.

questions.solution:
1. Block multiply: $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}I&2B\\0&I\end{pmatrix}$, and by induction $M^k=\begin{pmatrix}I&kB\\0&I\end{pmatrix}$.
2. The $(1,4)$ entry of $M^5$ is $5B_{12}=5\cdot2=10$.

questions.stem: $A$ ($p\times p$) and $D$ ($q\times q$) are invertible and $B$ is $p\times q$. The inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}$ is

options.why: Copied the scalar rule for $\begin{pmatrix}1&b\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$; top-right gives $-AB+BD^{-1}\neq0$ in general.
Sign error: the top-right block becomes $2BD^{-1}$, not $0$.
Multiply out: top-right block $A(-A^{-1}BD^{-1})+BD^{-1}=0$.
Wrong order: $D^{-1}BA^{-1}$ is not even defined unless $p=q$; block products keep their order.

questions.solution: Solve $\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&D\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}X&Y\\0&Z\end{pmatrix}=I$: $X=A^{-1}$, $Z=D^{-1}$, $AY+BZ=0\Rightarrow Y=-A^{-1}BD^{-1}$.

traps.why: Added the block determinants ($5+2$) instead of multiplying.
Used only the top-left block.

questions.solution:
1. Block upper triangular: $\det=\det\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}\det\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$.
2. $=5\cdot2=10$. The top-right block does not matter.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be $m\times n$ with columns $a_1,\dots,a_n$ and $B$ be $n\times p$ with rows $b_1^T,\dots,b_n^T$. Which statements are true?

options.text: The $i$-th row of $AB$ is the $i$-th row of $A$ times $B$
options.why: Each row of the product is a combination of the rows of $B$.
Order reversed: $b_ia_i^T$ is $p\times m$, the shape of $(AB)^T$; in fact $\sum b_ia_i^T=(AB)^T$.

options.text: The $j$-th column of $AB$ is $A$ times the $j$-th column of $B$
options.why: Each column of the product is a combination of the columns of $A$.
Column-times-row expansion: a sum of $n$ outer products, each $m\times p$.

questions.solution: Three views of $AB$: entries (row·column), columns ($A\cdot$column of $B$), rows (row of $A\cdot B$), plus outer products $\sum a_ib_i^T$.

questions.stem: $A$ is $3\times2$, $B$ is $2\times4$, $C$ is $4\times3$. Which expression is **not** defined?

options.why: $(4\times3)(3\times2)(2\times4)$ gives a $4\times4$ matrix.
$(3\times2)(2\times4)(4\times3)$ gives a $3\times3$ matrix.
$(3\times2)(4\times3)$: inner sizes $2\neq4$, so $AC$ is undefined.
$(2\times4)(4\times3)(3\times2)$ gives a $2\times2$ matrix.

questions.solution: Check adjacent inner dimensions. Cyclic shifts of $ABC$ are all defined here; $ACB$ breaks at $A\cdot C$.

questions.stem: Let $A$ and $B$ be invertible $n\times n$ matrices. Which statements are true?

options.why: Transpose $AA^{-1}=I$ to get $(A^{-1})^TA^T=I$.
Order must reverse: $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$, since $AB\,B^{-1}A^{-1}=I$.
$(XY)^T=Y^TX^T$ with $X=A$, $Y=B^T$.

questions.solution: Transpose and inverse both reverse the order of a product. Neither distributes the way you want over a sum, and inverse not at all.

questions.stem: $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix with $A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$. Find the $(1,1)$ entry of $(2A)^{-1}$.

traps.why: Used $(2A)^{-1}=2A^{-1}$: multiplied instead of dividing.
Took the reciprocal of a single entry, $1/(2\cdot4)$; entries of an inverse are not reciprocals of entries.
Computed $A$ and reported the $(1,1)$ entry of $2A$, not of its inverse.

questions.solution:
1. $(cA)^{-1}=\tfrac1c A^{-1}$.
2. $(2A)^{-1}=\tfrac12\begin{pmatrix}4&2\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$, so the $(1,1)$ entry is $2$.

questions.stem: For invertible $n\times n$ matrices $A$ and $B$, the matrix $\big((AB)^T\big)^{-1}$ equals

options.why: Dropped the transpose. This is $(BA)^{-1}$, not related to $(AB)^T$.
This is $(AB)^{-1}$; the transpose was ignored.
Reversed the order only once; transpose and inverse each reverse, so the net order is $A$ then $B$.
$(AB)^T=B^TA^T$; its inverse is $(A^T)^{-1}(B^T)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^T(B^{-1})^T$. Two reversals restore the order.

questions.solution:
1. $(AB)^T=B^TA^T$.
2. $(B^TA^T)^{-1}=(A^T)^{-1}(B^T)^{-1}$.
3. $(A^T)^{-1}=(A^{-1})^T$. Numerical check with $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\3&1\end{pmatrix}$ confirms only $(A^{-1})^T(B^{-1})^T$.

questions.stem: A square matrix $A$ satisfies $A^2-3A+2I=0$. Which statements are true?

options.why: $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}$ also satisfies the equation; only the eigenvalues are restricted to $\{1,2\}$.
Sign slip when moving terms: $A(A-3I)=-2I$, so this is $-A^{-1}$.
Directly from $A(3I-A)=2I$.
Rearrange: $A(3I-A)=2I$, so $A\cdot\tfrac12(3I-A)=I$.

questions.solution:
1. $A^2-3A=-2I\Rightarrow A(3I-A)=2I$.
2. Hence $A^{-1}=\tfrac12(3I-A)$.
3. Eigenvalues satisfy $\lambda^2-3\lambda+2=0$, so each is 1 or 2, but they may be mixed.

questions.stem: Let $A$ be an invertible $n\times n$ real matrix and $c\neq0,\pm1$ a scalar. Which statements are true?

options.why: Reverse the order of the product $A^T\cdot A$: $(A^TA)^{-1}=A^{-1}(A^T)^{-1}$. Valid because $A$ is square and invertible.
$(cA)(cA^{-1})=c^2I\neq I$ (since $c\neq\pm1$); the correct inverse is $\tfrac1cA^{-1}$.

questions.solution: Inverse of a product reverses order; a scalar factor inverts to $1/c$. Symmetry passes to the inverse.

2. $\operatorname{rank}(A-I)=1\Rightarrow$ GM $=1<2$: not diagonalizable.

questions.stem: A $4\times4$ matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-1)^2(\lambda-3)^2$, with $\operatorname{rank}(A-I)=2$ and $\operatorname{rank}(A-3I)=3$. Which statements are true?

options.why: Equated GM with $\operatorname{rank}(A-3I)$; GM $=n-\operatorname{rank}=1$ (and GM can never exceed AM $=2$).
$0$ is not a root of the characteristic polynomial; $\det A=1\cdot1\cdot3\cdot3=9$.
GM $=4-\operatorname{rank}(A-I)=4-2=2$.
GM of $\lambda=3$ is $4-3=1<2=$ AM.

questions.solution: GM $=n-\operatorname{rank}(A-\lambda I)$: GM(1) $=2$, GM(3) $=1$. Diagonalizable needs GM $=$ AM for every eigenvalue.

questions.stem: Find the geometric multiplicity of $\lambda=4$ for $$A=\begin{pmatrix}4&1&0&0&0\\0&4&0&0&0\\0&0&4&0&0\\0&0&0&4&0\\0&0&0&0&9\end{pmatrix}.$$

traps.why: Reported $\operatorname{rank}(A-4I)=2$; GM is $5-2$.
Equated GM with AM $=4$; the $1$ above the diagonal removes one eigenvector.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\1&2&1\\1&1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Which vectors are eigenvectors of $A$?

options.why: Every row sums to 4, so $A(1,1,1)^T=4(1,1,1)^T$.
A non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector: $A(2,2,2)^T=8(1,1,1)^T=4(2,2,2)^T$.

questions.solution: Compute $Av$ and test proportionality. Don't skip the scaled vector: scaling preserves the eigenvector property.

questions.stem: Find the smallest eigenvalue of $$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\3&2&1\\2&2&2\end{pmatrix}.$$

traps.why: Found $\det A=0$ (so $0$ is an eigenvalue) and stopped; the third eigenvalue is $5-6-0=-1$.
Sign slip: used trace $-$ row sum as $6-5$.

questions.solution:
1. Row sums are all 6: eigenvalue 6 with $(1,1,1)^T$.
2. $\det A=1(4-2)-2(6-2)+3(6-4)=0$: eigenvalue 0.
3. Trace $5$: third eigenvalue $5-6-0=-1$.

questions.stem: Which vector is an eigenvector of $\begin{pmatrix}4&1\\2&3\end{pmatrix}$ for the eigenvalue $2$?

options.why: Swapped the components: $A(2,-1)^T=(7,1)^T$.
Sign slip in $(A-2I)x=0$: $A(1,2)^T=(6,8)^T$, not a multiple.
This is the eigenvector for $\lambda=5$ (equal row sums 5), not 2.

questions.solution: $A-2I=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$, so $2x+y=0$: $(1,-2)^T$. Verify with $Av$.

questions.stem: $A$ is an invertible $n\times n$ matrix in which every row sums to $3$. Which statements are true?

options.why: $A^2\mathbf{1}=A(3\mathbf{1})=9\mathbf{1}$.
Row sums say nothing about column sums: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&0\end{pmatrix}$ has row sums $3,3$ but column sums $4,2$.
$A\mathbf{1}=3\mathbf{1}$ where $\mathbf{1}$ is the all-ones vector.
From $A\mathbf{1}=3\mathbf{1}$: $A^{-1}\mathbf{1}=\tfrac13\mathbf{1}$.

questions.solution: Equal row sums $s$ means $\mathbf{1}$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $s$; powers and inverses keep it with $s^k$, $1/s$.

questions.stem: For what value of $k$ is $(2,1)^T$ an eigenvector of $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&k\\1&4\end{pmatrix}$?

traps.why: Set $4+k=6$, using the eigenvalue as the first component; the first component must be $\lambda\cdot2=12$.
Sign slip solving $4+k=12$.

questions.solution:
1. $A(2,1)^T=(4+k,\,6)^T$.
2. Second component: $6=\lambda\cdot1\Rightarrow\lambda=6$.
3. First: $4+k=6\cdot2=12\Rightarrow k=8$.

questions.stem: $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix with $\det A=2$. Which statements are true?

options.why: $(-1)^3\det A=-2$; for odd $n$ the sign flips.
Dropped the transpose factor: $\det(A^T)=\det A$, so $\det(A^2A^T)=2^3=8$.
$2^3\cdot2=16$; every one of the 3 rows is scaled.

questions.solution: Use $\det(cA)=c^n\det A$, $\det(A^{-1})=1/\det A$, $\det(A^T)=\det A$ and multiplicativity.

questions.stem: A $2\times2$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $3$. Which statements are true?

options.why: Cayley–Hamilton: $A$ satisfies its characteristic polynomial $(\lambda-1)(\lambda-3)$.
Determinant is not additive: $\det(A+I)=(1+1)(3+1)=8$.

questions.solution: Evaluate the polynomial at each eigenvalue and multiply; never add $\det$'s.

questions.stem: $P$ is a real $n\times n$ matrix with $P^2=P$, $P^T=P$ and $\operatorname{rank}P=r$, where $0<r<n$. Which statements are true?

options.why: $r<n$ means eigenvalue 0 is present, so $\det P=0$. Only $P=I$ has determinant 1.
Eigenvalue 1 appears $r$ times (the column space), 0 appears $n-r$ times; trace sums them.
$\lambda^2=\lambda$ from $P^2=P$.
$x=Px+(I-P)x$ with orthogonal parts, so $\lVert x\rVert^2=\lVert Px\rVert^2+\lVert(I-P)x\rVert^2$.

questions.solution: An orthogonal projection splits $\mathbb{R}^n$ into its column space (eigenvalue 1) and the orthogonal complement (eigenvalue 0). Rank $=$ trace; never shrinks to more than length.

questions.stem: Let $P$ be the orthogonal projection onto the line spanned by $a=(1,2,2)^T$. For $x=(3,0,3)^T$, find the third component of $Px$.

traps.why: Used $aa^Tx$ without dividing by $a^Ta=9$.
Divided by $\lVert a\rVert=3$ instead of $\lVert a\rVert^2=9$.

questions.solution:
1. $Px=\dfrac{a^Tx}{a^Ta}a=\dfrac{3+0+6}{9}a=a$.
2. $Px=(1,2,2)^T$; third component $2$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $b=(1,2,4)^T$. Let $p$ be the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A$. Find $\lVert b-p\rVert^2$.

traps.why: Projected with $(b^Ta_i)a_i$ without dividing by $a_i^Ta_i$ ($3$ and $2$).
Reported $\lVert p\rVert^2$ instead of the residual $\lVert b-p\rVert^2$.

questions.solution:
1. Columns $a_1=(1,1,1)$, $a_2=(0,1,-1)$ are orthogonal, so $p=\frac{7}{3}a_1+\frac{-2}{2}a_2=(\tfrac73,\tfrac43,\tfrac{10}3)$.
2. $b-p=(-\tfrac43,\tfrac23,\tfrac23)$, orthogonal to both columns.
3. $\lVert b-p\rVert^2=\tfrac{16+4+4}{9}=\tfrac83\approx2.667$.

questions.stem: Which matrix is an **orthogonal** projection?

options.why: Its square is $0$ (nilpotent), not itself; trace 0 already rules it out as a rank-1 projection.
Symmetric and orthogonal, but its square is $I$: a reflection, eigenvalues $\pm1$.
Symmetric and $P^2=P$: projection onto the line through $(1,1)$.
Idempotent but not symmetric: an oblique projection.

questions.solution: Orthogonal projection $\iff P^2=P$ and $P^T=P$. Test both.

questions.stem: $A$ is a real $5\times2$ matrix with independent columns and $P=A(A^TA)^{-1}A^T$. Which statements are true?

options.text: $P$ has eigenvalue 1 with multiplicity 3 and eigenvalue 0 with multiplicity 2
options.why: Swapped the counts: eigenvalue 1 lives on the 2-dim column space, 0 on its 3-dim complement; trace $=2=$ rank confirms.
$A$ is not square, so $A^{-1}$ does not exist and the inverse cannot be split. $P=I$ only when $A$ is square and invertible.
$A(A^TA)^{-1}A^TA=A$; vectors already in the column space are unchanged.
$P$ projects onto the 2-dimensional column space of $A$.

questions.solution: $P$ is symmetric and idempotent with rank equal to $\operatorname{rank}A=2$. It equals $I$ only if the columns span $\mathbb{R}^5$.

questions.stem: $Q$ is a real orthogonal $n\times n$ matrix. Which statements are true?

options.why: $\det(Q^TQ)=(\det Q)^2=1$.
Definition: $Q^TQ=I$.
Rotation by $90^\circ$, $\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, has eigenvalues $\pm i$. Only $|\lambda|=1$ is guaranteed.
$\lVert Qx\rVert^2=x^TQ^TQx=x^Tx$.

questions.solution: Orthogonal: $Q^TQ=I$. Length preserving, $|\det|=1$, eigenvalues on the unit circle (real ones are $\pm1$).

questions.stem: For which $(a,b)$ is $Q=\begin{pmatrix}0.6&a\\0.8&b\end{pmatrix}$ orthogonal?

options.why: Orthogonal to the first column but length 10, not 1.
Second column is a unit vector orthogonal to $(0.6,0.8)$: $-0.48+0.48=0$.
Unit length but not orthogonal: $0.48+0.48\neq0$.
Repeats the first column; $\det Q=0$.

questions.solution: Columns must be orthonormal: unit length and mutually orthogonal.

questions.stem: $Q$ is a real $4\times4$ orthogonal matrix. Find $|\det(3Q)|$.

traps.why: Used $c$ instead of $c^n$: $3\cdot|\det Q|$.
Multiplied $3$ by $n=4$ instead of raising it to the 4th power.

questions.stem: $Q_1$ and $Q_2$ are real orthogonal $n\times n$ matrices. Which statements are true?

options.why: $Q_1=Q_2=I$ gives $2I$, which stretches lengths by 2.
$Q_1^T=Q_1^{-1}$, and the inverse of an orthogonal matrix is orthogonal.
$Q_1^2=Q_1^TQ_1=I$: a symmetric orthogonal matrix is a reflection (eigenvalues $\pm1$).

questions.solution: Orthogonal matrices form a group under multiplication (products, inverses, transposes), not under addition.

questions.stem: Let $u=\tfrac13(1,2,2)^T$ and $H=I_3-2uu^T$. Find $\operatorname{tr}H$.

traps.why: Ignored the $-2uu^T$ term or assumed $\operatorname{tr}(uu^T)=0$.
Reported $\det H$; $H$ is a reflection with eigenvalues $-1,1,1$.

questions.solution:
1. $u$ is a unit vector, so $\operatorname{tr}(uu^T)=u^Tu=1$.
2. $\operatorname{tr}H=3-2=1$. Eigenvalues: $-1$ (along $u$), $1,1$; $H$ is orthogonal and symmetric.

questions.stem: The quadratic form $Q(x,y)=3x^2+4xy+2y^2$ is

options.why: Matrix $\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$: leading minors $3>0$, $6-4=2>0$.

options.text: positive semidefinite but not positive definite
options.why: That needs $\det=0$; here $\det=2>0$.
Diagonal entries are positive, so $Q(1,0)=3>0$.
Put the full coefficient 4 off the diagonal: $\begin{pmatrix}3&4\\4&2\end{pmatrix}$ has $\det=-10$. The cross term must be halved.

questions.solution:
1. Symmetric matrix: $\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$ (cross coefficient split as $2+2$).
2. Minors $3$, $2$: positive definite. Eigenvalues $(5\pm\sqrt{17})/2>0$.

questions.stem: For $k>0$, the form $Q(x,y)=x^2+2kxy+4y^2$ is positive semidefinite but not positive definite. Find $k$.

traps.why: Did not halve the cross term: used $\begin{pmatrix}1&2k\\2k&4\end{pmatrix}$, giving $4-4k^2=0$.
Solved $k^2=4$ as $k=4$, forgetting the square root.

questions.solution:
1. Matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\k&4\end{pmatrix}$.
2. PSD but singular: $\det=4-k^2=0\Rightarrow k=2$.
3. Then $Q=(x+2y)^2\ge0$, zero along $x=-2y$.

questions.stem: $A$ is a real $m\times n$ matrix and $G=A^TA$. Which statements are true?

options.text: $G$ is positive definite if and only if the columns of $A$ are linearly independent
options.why: $x^TGx=0\iff Ax=0$, which forces $x=0$ exactly when the columns are independent.
$x^TGx=\lVert Ax\rVert^2\ge0$.

options.text: $AA^T$ and $A^TA$ have the same non-zero eigenvalues
options.why: If $A^TAv=\lambda v$ with $\lambda\neq0$, then $AA^T(Av)=\lambda(Av)$ and $Av\neq0$.
$\operatorname{rank}G\le m<n$, so the $n\times n$ matrix $G$ is singular. E.g. $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\0&1&1\end{pmatrix}$ gives $\det G=0$.

questions.solution: Gram matrices are always PSD; PD exactly when $A$ has full column rank, which needs $m\ge n$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0\\-1&2&-1\\0&-1&2\end{pmatrix}$. Which statements are true?

options.why: Leading principal minors $2$, $3$, $4$ are all positive.
Multiplied the diagonal entries; $A$ is not triangular. $\det A=4$.

options.text: $x^TAx<0$ for some $x$, because of the negative off-diagonal entries
options.why: Signs of off-diagonal entries do not decide definiteness; $x^TAx=x_1^2+(x_1-x_2)^2+(x_2-x_3)^2+x_3^2>0$ for $x\ne0$.
Equivalent to positive definiteness for a symmetric matrix (they are $2-\sqrt2,\,2,\,2+\sqrt2$).

questions.solution: Minors: $2$; $4-1=3$; $\det A=2(4-1)+1(-2-0)=4$. All positive, so PD.

questions.stem: Which matrix is positive definite?

options.why: Eigenvalue 0: only positive semidefinite.
Positive diagonal is necessary, not sufficient: $\det=8-9=-1<0$, indefinite.
Minors $2>0$, $4-1=3>0$; eigenvalues $1,3$.
Positive entries do not imply PD: eigenvalues $3,-1$.

questions.solution: For $2\times2$ symmetric: PD iff $a_{11}>0$ and $\det>0$.

questions.stem: Find the maximum of $x^TAx$ over unit vectors $x\in\mathbb{R}^2$, where $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\1&3\end{pmatrix}$.

traps.why: Took the largest diagonal entry; that is only $x^TAx$ at $x=e_1$.
Plugged in $x=(1,1)^T$ without normalising: $\lVert x\rVert^2=2$.

questions.solution:
1. Eigenvalues: $3\pm1$, i.e. $4,2$.
2. Max of the Rayleigh quotient $=\lambda_{\max}=4$, at $x=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,1)^T$.

questions.stem: Find the minimum of $5x^2+4xy+2y^2$ subject to $x^2+y^2=1$.

traps.why: Took the smaller diagonal coefficient (value at $(0,1)$), not the smallest eigenvalue.
Did not halve the cross term: used $\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\4&2\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.solution:
1. Matrix $\begin{pmatrix}5&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$: trace 7, det 6, eigenvalues $6,1$.
2. Minimum on the unit circle $=\lambda_{\min}=1$, at $x\propto(1,-2)$.

questions.stem: $A$ is a real symmetric $3\times3$ matrix with eigenvalues $-2, 1, 5$, and $R(x)=\dfrac{x^TAx}{x^Tx}$ for $x\neq0$. Which statements are true?

options.why: Minimum is $\lambda_{\min}$.
Rayleigh quotient maximum is $\lambda_{\max}$, attained at its eigenvector.

options.text: The maximum of $x^TAx$ over $\lVert x\rVert\le2$ is $10$
options.why: $x^TAx$ scales with $\lVert x\rVert^2$, not $\lVert x\rVert$: the maximum is $4\cdot5=20$.
Take $x$ an eigenvector for $\lambda=1$; $R$ takes every value in $[-2,5]$.

questions.solution: $\lambda_{\min}\le R(x)\le\lambda_{\max}$. On a sphere of radius $r$, multiply by $r^2$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\operatorname{diag}(2,-3,1)$. The maximum of $x^TAx$ over unit vectors $x\in\mathbb{R}^3$ is

options.why: Took the largest eigenvalue in absolute value (spectral norm), but $x^TAx$ keeps the sign.
Averaged the eigenvalues; that is $\operatorname{tr}A/3$, not the maximum.
That is the minimum, $\lambda_{\min}$.

questions.solution: For symmetric $A$, $\max_{\lVert x\rVert=1}x^TAx=\lambda_{\max}=2$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$ and consider $f(x)=x^TAx$ on the unit circle $\lVert x\rVert=1$. Which statements are true?

options.why: That is the eigenvector for $\lambda=1$, where the minimum occurs; the maximum is at $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,1)^T$ (row sums equal 3).

options.text: The minimum of $f$ is $2$, the smallest diagonal entry
options.why: Diagonal entries are values of $f$, not its minimum; the minimum is $\lambda_{\min}=1$ at $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(1,-1)^T$.

options.text: $f(e_1)=2$ lies between the minimum and maximum
options.why: $f(e_1)=a_{11}=2\in[1,3]$; diagonal entries always lie in $[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]$.
Eigenvalues $3$ and $1$; maximum is $\lambda_{\max}=3$.

questions.solution: Extremes of $x^TAx$ on the unit sphere are the extreme eigenvalues; diagonal entries sit between them.

questions.stem: Write $A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\6&5\end{pmatrix}=LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular and $U$ upper triangular. Find $u_{22}$.

traps.why: Copied $a_{22}$ without eliminating.
Added instead of subtracting: $5+3\cdot1$.

questions.stem: Find $u_{33}$ in the Doolittle factorization $A=LU$ ($L$ unit lower triangular) of $$A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&0\\2&5&1\\0&3&4\end{pmatrix}.$$

traps.why: Copied $a_{33}$; row 3 still has to be reduced by $3\times$ the new row 2.
Added instead of subtracting: $4+3\cdot1$.

questions.stem: Which matrix has **no** LU factorization (unit lower $L$, upper $U$) without row exchanges?

options.why: Singular but already upper triangular: $L=I$, $U=A$.
First pivot is 0 and the entry below is non-zero: $l_{21}u_{11}=1$ is impossible with $u_{11}=a_{11}=0$.
Assumed singular means no LU; $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $U=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ works.

questions.solution: LU without pivoting fails when a zero pivot meets a non-zero entry below it. Singularity alone is not the obstacle.

questions.stem: $A=LU$ where $L$ is unit lower triangular and $U$ is upper triangular, all $n\times n$. Which statements are true?

options.text: Every invertible matrix has such a factorization without row exchanges
options.why: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is invertible but has a zero first pivot; it needs $PA=LU$.

options.text: $\det A$ equals the product of the diagonal entries of $U$
options.why: $\det L=1$, and $U$ is triangular.

options.text: $Ax=b$ can be solved by forward substitution in $Ly=b$, then back substitution in $Ux=y$
options.why: That is the purpose of the factorization: two triangular solves.

options.text: $A$ is invertible if and only if every diagonal entry of $U$ is non-zero
options.why: Follows from $\det A=\prod u_{ii}$.

questions.solution: LU turns one solve into two triangular solves; existence without pivoting needs non-zero leading pivots.

questions.stem: Given $L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\2&1&0\\-1&3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $U=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&1\\0&1&-1\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix}$, find the $(3,3)$ entry of $A=LU$.

traps.why: Took only $l_{33}u_{33}$; row 3 of $L$ has three non-zero entries.
Sign slip: used $u_{23}=+1$, giving $-1+3+4$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}=LU$ with $L$ unit lower triangular. Which statements are true?

options.why: Added instead of subtracting: $4+3\cdot2$.
Product of $U$'s diagonal: $1\cdot(-2)$; matches $4-6$.
Multiplier $a_{21}/a_{11}=3/1$.

questions.stem: Find the largest singular value of $A=\begin{pmatrix}3&0\\4&5\end{pmatrix}$ (to two decimals).

traps.why: Took the largest eigenvalue (diagonal of a triangular matrix); singular values differ from eigenvalues for non-symmetric $A$.
Forgot the square root of the eigenvalue of $A^TA$.

questions.solution:
1. $A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}25&20\\20&25\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvalues $45, 5$.
2. $\sigma_1=\sqrt{45}\approx6.708$, $\sigma_2=\sqrt5$. Check: $\sigma_1\sigma_2=15=|\det A|$.

questions.stem: Let $u=(1,2,2)^T$, $v=(3,4)^T$ and $A=uv^T$ (a $3\times2$ matrix). Which statements are true?

options.text: The only non-zero singular value of $A$ is $15$
options.why: $\sigma=\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert=3\cdot5$.

options.text: The singular values of $A$ are $3$ and $5$
options.why: Listed the two norms separately; the single non-zero singular value is their product.
Every column is a multiple of $u$.
$A^TA=\lVert u\rVert^2vv^T=9vv^T$, eigenvalues $9\cdot25=225$ and $0$.

questions.solution: $A=\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert\,\hat u\hat v^T$ is already an SVD with one singular value $15$.

questions.stem: Which statements about singular values are true?

options.text: A symmetric positive semidefinite matrix with eigenvalues $4,1,0$ has singular values $4,1,0$
options.why: For symmetric PSD $A$, $A^TA=A^2$ has eigenvalues $\lambda^2$, so $\sigma=\lambda$.

options.text: $\max_{\lVert x\rVert=1}\lVert Ax\rVert$ equals the largest singular value
options.why: $\lVert Ax\rVert^2=x^TA^TAx\le\lambda_{\max}(A^TA)=\sigma_1^2$.

options.text: A $3\times3$ matrix with singular values $4,1,0$ has rank 3
options.why: Counted all singular values; rank equals the number of non-zero ones, here 2.

options.text: A symmetric matrix with eigenvalues $3$ and $-2$ has singular values $3$ and $-2$
options.why: Singular values are never negative; for symmetric $A$ they are $|\lambda|$: $3$ and $2$.

questions.solution: $\sigma_i=\sqrt{\lambda_i(A^TA)}\ge0$. Symmetric: $\sigma=|\lambda|$; symmetric PSD: $\sigma=\lambda$.

questions.stem: A real $3\times3$ matrix $A$ has singular values $3, 2, 1$. Find $\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^2$ (the squared Frobenius norm).

traps.why: Added the singular values instead of their squares.
Squared the sum of singular values: $(3+2+1)^2$.

questions.solution: $\sum a_{ij}^2=\operatorname{tr}(A^TA)=\sum\sigma_i^2=9+4+1=14$.

questions.stem: The singular values of $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ are

options.why: Used the column norms; the columns are equal, so the matrix has rank 1, not 2.
Forgot the square root of the eigenvalues of $A^TA$.
$A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $4,0$; square roots $2,0$.
Read off entries as if $A$ were diagonal.

questions.solution:
1. $A^TA=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$, eigenvalues $4,0$.
2. $\sigma=2,0$; rank 1.

questions.stem: $A$ is a real $m\times n$ matrix of rank $r$ with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\dots$. Which statements are true?

options.text: For square $A$, the singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues
options.why: Only for normal (e.g. symmetric) $A$. $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has eigenvalues $0,0$ but singular values $1,0$.

options.text: Exactly $r$ singular values of $A$ are non-zero
options.why: $\operatorname{rank}(A^TA)=\operatorname{rank}A=r$, so $A^TA$ has $r$ non-zero eigenvalues.
$\sigma_1$ is the largest stretch factor of $A$.

options.text: $A$ and $A^T$ have the same non-zero singular values
options.why: $A^TA$ and $AA^T$ share their non-zero eigenvalues.

questions.solution: Singular values come from $A^TA$, not from the characteristic polynomial of $A$; they match $|\lambda|$ only for normal matrices.
